entry: Wave of liberal democratic movements that toppled most Marxist–Leninist governments in the Eastern Bloc. Also called the Fall of Communism, the uprisings began with a general strike in Poland on August 14, 1980, which led to the independent trade union Solidarity, whose peak membership reached 10 million. Poland held elections on June 4, 1989, that dissolved its communist government, and Hungary began dismantling its section of the [[Iron Curtain]]. The opening of a border gate between Austria and Hungary set off a chain reaction across the Eastern Bloc. The [[Fall of the Berlin Wall|fall of the Berlin Wall]] in November 1989 led to German reunification in 1990. The revolutions were a key factor in the dissolution of the [[Soviet Union]] in December 1991, and the [[Cold War]] is considered to have ended at the Malta Summit on December 3, 1989.

Seventh studio album by the English rock band [[The Beatles|the Beatles]]. *Revolver* was released on August 5, 1966, as the band's final recording project before it retired from live performance. The songs reflect interest in LSD, Eastern philosophy and the avant-garde, and include "Tomorrow Never Knows" and "Love You To," a foray into Hindustani classical music. The album topped the Record Retailer chart in the UK for seven weeks. Its cover, designed by Klaus Voormann, won the 1967 Grammy Award for Best Album Cover, Graphic Arts. The album expanded the boundaries of [[Pop music|pop music]] and inspired the development of psychedelic rock.

Repeating [[Handgun|handgun]] with a revolving cylinder of chambers, each holding one cartridge. Most models hold six cartridges before reloading, so revolvers are often called six shooters or sixguns. Cocking the hammer, by hand or through the trigger pull, rotates the cylinder to align a chamber with the barrel. Revolver actions also appear on some [[Rifle|rifles]] and [[Shotgun|shotguns]]. Revolvers have been largely surpassed by semi-automatic pistols, but they remain popular as backup and off-duty handguns among American law enforcement officers. Famous models include the Colt Single Action Army and the Smith & Wesson Model 29 of *Dirty Harry* fame.

Capital and largest city of [[Iceland]]. It lies on the southern shore of Faxaflói bay in southwest Iceland and is the world's northernmost capital of a sovereign state. It has about 140,000 residents as of 2026, and the Capital Region has about 252,000, approximately 64% of Iceland's population. According to the *Landnámabók*, settlement began when Ingólfur Arnarson arrived from [[Norway]] in 874. The city was officially founded in 1786 as a trading town and grew into the center of the nation's cultural, economic and governmental life. Its name, meaning bay of smoke, is said to refer to steam from hot springs.

Characteristic number in [[Fluid dynamics|fluid dynamics]] that measures the ratio of inertial to viscous forces. It helps predict flow patterns: low Reynolds numbers favor smooth, laminar (sheet-like) flow, while high values tend toward [[Turbulence|turbulence]], in which eddy currents churn the flow and, in liquids, increase the chances of cavitation. The number predicts the transition from laminar to turbulent flow and is used to scale experiments, such as between a model aircraft in a wind tunnel and its full-size version. Pipe flows are typically classified as laminar below Re = 2,300, transitional between 2,300 and 4,000, and turbulent above 4,000, though thresholds vary with geometry and disturbances. George Stokes introduced the concept in 1851. Arnold Sommerfeld named the number in 1908 after Osborne Reynolds, who popularized its use in 1883.

1924 composition for solo piano and jazz band by [[George Gershwin]]. Commissioned by bandleader Paul Whiteman for a concert titled "An Experiment in Modern Music," the work combines elements of [[Classical music|classical music]] with jazz-influenced effects. It was premiered on February 12, 1924, at Aeolian Hall in New York City, with Gershwin at the piano. Gershwin had only five weeks to compose it. Ferde Grofé orchestrated the rhapsody several times, including a 1924 original scoring, a 1926 pit orchestra scoring and a 1942 symphonic scoring. It inaugurated a new era in American music, established Gershwin's reputation and became one of the most popular of all concert works. According to Frederic D. Schwarz in *American Heritage* magazine, its opening clarinet glissando is as instantly recognizable to concert audiences as the opening of Beethoven's *Fifth Symphony*.

Genus of large, flightless South American ratite birds. Rheas are distantly related to the two African [[Ostrich|ostriches]] and to the [[Emu|emu]] of Australia. Two species are generally recognized: the greater rhea (*Rhea americana*) and the lesser, or Darwin's, rhea (*Rhea pennata*). Large males of the greater rhea can reach 170 cm (67 in) tall at the head and weigh up to 40 kg (88 lb). Their wings, spread while running like sails, are large for a flightless bird. Rheas inhabit open grasslands and [[Pampas|pampas]], mostly in lowlands. The International Union for Conservation of Nature rates the greater rhea as near-threatened, while Darwin's rhea is of least concern. The feral population of the greater rhea in [[Germany]] appears to be growing. The name was adopted in 1752 after the Greek Titan Rhea.

Rare, silvery-gray, heavy transition metal (symbol Re, atomic number 75) of group 7 in the [[Periodic table|periodic table]]. Rhenium is one of the rarest elements in the Earth's crust. It has one of the highest melting and boiling points of any element and resembles manganese and technetium chemically. It is mainly obtained as a by-product of refining [[Molybdenum|molybdenum]] and [[Copper|copper]] ores. Nickel-based superalloys containing up to 6% rhenium are used in the combustion chambers and turbine blades of [[Jet engine|jet engines]], the element's largest single use. Rhenium is also an excellent catalyst, as in the reforming of naphtha for [[Gasoline|gasoline]]. The element was named after the [[Rhine]], from which the earliest samples were obtained. Masataka Ogawa announced an element in 1908 that he had mistakenly identified as element 43, but the element was rediscovered in 1925 by Walter Noddack, Ida Noddack and Otto Berg.

Species of [[Old World monkey|Old World monkey]] (*Macaca mulatta*) with the widest geographic range of any non-human primate. Generally brown or gray, it measures 47–53 cm (19–21 in) in length, with a tail of 20.7–22.9 cm (8.1–9.0 in), and weighs 5.3–7.7 kg (12–17 lb). It is native to South, Central and Southeast Asia and occupies a wide range of altitudes and habitats. Mostly herbivorous, it lives in gregarious troops of 20–200 individuals with matrilineal social groups. Because it is easy to keep and physiologically close to humans, it has been used extensively in research, contributing to vaccines for [[Rabies|rabies]], [[Smallpox|smallpox]] and [[Polio|polio]] and to antiretroviral medication for [[HIV/AIDS|HIV/AIDS]]. A rhesus macaque became the first primate astronaut in 1948. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists the species as Least Concern.

Art of persuasion, one of the three ancient arts of discourse (the *trivium*) of classical antiquity, along with grammar and [[Logic|logic]]. As an academic discipline in the humanities, rhetoric studies the techniques that speakers and writers use to inform, persuade and motivate audiences. [[Aristotle]] defined it as "the faculty of observing in any given case the available means of persuasion" and identified three audience appeals: *logos*, *pathos* and *ethos*. The five canons of rhetoric, first codified in classical Rome, are *inventio*, *dispositio*, *elocutio*, *memoria* and *pronuntiatio*. From ancient Greece to the late 19th century, rhetoric was central to Western and Islamic education. [[Plato]] criticized the [[Sophist|Sophists]] for using it to deceive rather than to discover truth, and in *Gorgias* he described it as a form of flattery, a view some scholars contest. Modern scholars study rhetoric across the sciences, fine art, journalism and digital media.

Long-term [[Autoimmune disease|autoimmune]] disorder that primarily affects the [[Joint|joints]]. It typically causes warm, swollen and painful joints, most often in the wrists and hands and often on both sides of the body. The immune system attacks the joints, thickening the joint capsule and affecting the underlying bone and [[Cartilage|cartilage]]. Treatment aims to reduce pain and inflammation. Drugs such as methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine may slow progression, and biological DMARDs are used when other treatments fail. About 17.6 million people had the disease worldwide as of 2020. Onset is most frequent during middle age, and women are affected 2.5 times more than men.

Major river of Western Europe, about 1,230 km (760 mi) long, flowing from the Swiss [[Alps|Alps]] to the [[North Sea|North Sea]]. It rises in the Swiss canton of Graubünden and forms parts of the borders of Switzerland, Liechtenstein and Austria before defining much of the Franco-German border. It then flows north through the German Rhineland and west into the Netherlands. Draining about 185,000 sq km, it is the second-longest river in Central and Western Europe, after the [[Danube|Danube]]. It contains the Rhine Falls, the most powerful waterfall in Europe. The Rhine and the Danube formed much of the northern inland boundary of the [[Roman Empire|Roman Empire]], and the river has long been a vital waterway for trade. Major cities on its banks include [[Cologne|Cologne]] and [[Rotterdam|Rotterdam]]. The International Commission for the Hydrology of the Rhine Basin contends that the river could experience a massive decrease in volume, or even dry up in drought, within 30 to 80 years as a result of the climate crisis.

Landlocked state in western [[Germany|Germany]]. It covers 19,846 sq km and has about 4.05 million residents, making it the ninth largest and sixth most populous of the 16 states. Mainz is the capital and largest city; other cities include Ludwigshafen am Rhein, Koblenz, Trier and Kaiserslautern. The state was established on August 30, 1946, by the French military administration from parts of Prussia, [[Hesse|Hesse]] and [[Bavaria|Bavaria]]. It became part of the Federal Republic of Germany in 1949. Its heritage includes the Palatinate winegrowing region, picturesque landscapes and many castles and palaces.

Family of large odd-toed ungulates (perissodactyls), *Rhinocerotidae*, with five living species. The black and white rhinoceroses are native to [[Africa|Africa]], while the Javan, Indian and Sumatran rhinoceroses are native to South and Southeast Asia. All living species weigh more than half a tonne as adults. They have one or two horns made of keratin, the material of hair and fingernails, over a thick protective skin formed from layers of collagen. Their diet is herbivorous, although the African species lack front teeth and pluck food with their lips. Poachers kill rhinos for their horns, which are sold on the [[Black market|black market]] at high prices, and most living species are endangered. Demand is driven mainly by China and Vietnam, where horn is used in [[Traditional Chinese medicine|traditional Chinese medicine]], although there is no good evidence of health benefits. The southern white rhinoceros recovered from near extinction in the early 20th century to over 18,000 individuals by the 2010s.

Diverse, species-rich [[Clade|clade]] of mostly unicellular [[Eukaryote|eukaryotes]]. Except for chlorarachniophytes and three species of the genus *Paulinella*, they are not photosynthetic, but many [[Foraminifera|Foraminifera]] and [[Radiolaria|Radiolaria]] have symbiotic relationships with unicellular algae. Most are amoeboid, with filose, reticulose or microtubule-supported pseudopods, and they lack clear morphological characters that define the group. Some possess mineral skeletons made of opal, celestite or calcite. Certain species form colonies about 1 cm in diameter and more than 1 m long. The three main groups are Cercozoa, Foraminifera and Radiolaria. Cavalier-Smith introduced the expanded group in 2002, and molecular phylogenetic studies have supported Rhizaria as a clade. Symbiotic forms contribute significantly to the total primary production of the ocean.

Smallest U.S. state by area, in the [[New England|New England]] region of the Northeastern United States. It borders [[Connecticut|Connecticut]] and [[Massachusetts|Massachusetts]]. Its population of slightly more than 1.11 million as of 2025 is the seventh-least of any state. Providence is the capital and largest city. Roger Williams founded it in 1636 as a haven for religious liberty, the first North American settlement with an explicitly secular government. The colony was the first to call for a Continental Congress, in 1774, and it was the last of the original 13 states to ratify the Constitution, on May 29, 1790.

Largest of Greece's Dodecanese islands and their historical capital. It is the ninth largest island in the Mediterranean Sea, located northeast of [[Crete|Crete]] and southeast of [[Athens|Athens]]. The city of Rhodes had 50,636 inhabitants in the 2011 census, and the island's population grew to 125,113 by 2022. In antiquity the island was famous for the [[Colossus of Rhodes|Colossus of Rhodes]], one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Knights of Saint John of Jerusalem ruled it from 1310 to 1522, a reference behind its nickname, the Island of the Knights. The medieval Old Town of the city is a [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage Site]]. Tourism routinely overwhelms the island's small population and limited infrastructure.

Unrecognized state in southern Africa, 1965–1979. It was the de facto successor to the self-governing colony of Southern Rhodesia after its unilateral declaration of independence from the [[United Kingdom|United Kingdom]] on November 11, 1965. The white-minority government conceded majority rule in 1978, but the [[Rhodesian Bush War|war]] continued. Under the Lancaster House Agreement of December 1979, elections were held and the territory became independent as Zimbabwe on April 18, 1980, under [[Robert Mugabe|Robert Mugabe]]. Critics note that Rhodesia's gains were shared unequally, as the black majority was excluded from political power. Supporters of the former government contrast its economy with later decline in Zimbabwe.

Civil conflict in southern Africa from July 1964 to December 1979. Also called the Second Chimurenga or the Zimbabwe War of Independence, it pitted the government of [[Rhodesia|Rhodesia]] against black nationalist guerrillas: the Zimbabwe African National Liberation Army, the military wing of [[Robert Mugabe|Robert Mugabe]]'s ZANU, and the Zimbabwe People's Revolutionary Army of Joshua Nkomo's ZAPU. Neither side achieved a military victory. The 1978 Internal Settlement brought universal suffrage in June 1979, but it did not win international recognition and the war continued. The Lancaster House Agreement of December 1979 led to elections in March 1980 and independence as [[Zimbabwe|Zimbabwe]] on April 18, 1980.

Very rare, silvery-white, hard, corrosion-resistant [[Transition metal|transition metal]] of the [[Platinum|platinum]] group (symbol Rh, atomic number 45). It was discovered in 1803 by William Hyde Wollaston in platinum ore and named for the rose color of one of its chlorine compounds, from the Greek *rhodon*, meaning rose. It is one of the rarest and most valuable precious metals, and it has only one naturally occurring isotope. Its major use, consuming about 80% of world production, is in the [[Catalytic converter|three-way catalytic converters]] of automobiles. Because it resists corrosion, rhodium is usually alloyed with [[Palladium|palladium]] or platinum for high-temperature coatings, and white gold jewelry is often plated with it. Rhodium detectors are used in nuclear reactors to measure neutron flux.

Very large genus of woody plants in the [[Ericaceae|heath family]], with about 1,024 species, though estimates vary from 850 to 1,200. The name comes from Greek words meaning rose and tree. Species are evergreen or deciduous shrubs and small trees, most native to eastern Asia and the Himalayan region. [[Azalea|Azaleas]] make up two subgenera and are distinguished by having five anthers per flower. Most species have brightly colored flowers that bloom from late winter through early summer. Several are national or state emblems, including the national flower of Nepal and the state flower of Washington. All parts of the plants contain grayanotoxins, which can cause gastrointestinal distress and neurological effects in humans and animals.

Equilateral [[Quadrilateral|quadrilateral]], a four-sided figure whose sides all have the same length. Also called a diamond or lozenge, it is a special case of a parallelogram and a kite. A rhombus with right angles is a [[Square|square]]. Its opposite angles are equal, its diagonals are perpendicular, and each diagonal bisects a pair of opposite angles. The name derives from the Greek *rhómbos*, meaning something that spins. [[Euclid|Euclid]] and [[Archimedes|Archimedes]] both used the word.

Herbaceous perennial of the genus *Rheum*, valued for its fleshy, sour, edible stalks. The large leaves contain high levels of [[Oxalic acid|oxalic acid]] and are poisonous and inedible. Culinary rhubarb developed from species and a possible hybrid grown in England and Scandinavia by the early 18th century. The stalks are botanically a vegetable but are often used as fruit, usually cooked with sugar in [[Pie|pies]], crumbles and other desserts. Hothouse rhubarb, forced in heated greenhouses, is brighter red, tenderer and sweeter than outdoor rhubarb and reaches markets in early spring.

Repetition of similar sounds, usually the same [[Phoneme|phonemes]], in the final stressed syllables of two or more words. In poetry and song, rhyme is most often used for musical or aesthetic effect at the ends of lines, and it also serves as a mnemonic device. In its specific sense, two words rhyme if their final stressed vowel and all following sounds are identical, as in *sight* and *flight*. Perfect rhymes are classified as single (masculine), double (feminine) or dactylic according to the position of the stressed syllable. The word may derive from Old French *rime*. The spelling *rhyme* was introduced at the start of the Modern English period through an association with Latin *rhythmus* that is likely etymologically incorrect. [[William Shakespeare|William Shakespeare]] often used rhyming couplets to mark the end of a scene in a play.

Popular music genre of African American origin, from the 1940s. The term was originally used by record companies for recordings marketed mainly to [[African Americans|African Americans]]. Commercial rhythm and blues of the 1950s through the 1970s usually featured a band with piano, one or two guitars, bass, drums and [[Saxophone|saxophones]]. Its lyrics often treat the African American experience, including racism, oppression and the quest for freedom and joy. Billboard journalist Jerry Wexler is credited with coining the term as a musical category. In the mid-1950s the term extended to electric [[Blues|blues]], gospel and soul, after the style had contributed to the development of [[Rock and roll|rock and roll]]. Contemporary R&B, which emerged in the late 1980s, combines the genre with [[Jazz|jazz]], soul, funk, disco and electronic elements.
